rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the eight-compound elution window while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. This scouting run will identify critical pairs and guide subsequent window, slope, and temperature adjustments.
Keep the gradient unchanged and raise temperature to test selectivity of the only unresolved pair. Higher temperature should also preserve the favorable last-elution time below 10 minutes.
Injection 2 reached the maximum CRF; shorten the gradient by one grid step to seek a faster fully resolved method. Monitor the first pair, whose resolution of 1.67 leaves the smallest margin.

Reduce the gradient slope to lie between injections 2 and 3, aiming to restore the first pair to R ≥ 1.5 while eluting faster than injection 2. The lower endpoint remains comfortably above the estimated last-peak elution fraction.

Shift the gradient window upward while preserving injection 4's slope to test whether initial weak-solvent time can be trimmed without losing resolution. The first pair remains the key constraint; injection 4 is the fully resolved fallback.

Test a cooler selectivity regime with a steeper gradient: the first pair may separate on the opposite side of a temperature-driven elution-order reversal. The shorter gradient and strong endpoint should limit the additional retention at lower temperature; injection 4 remains the fully resolved fallback.

Raise temperature one step while keeping injection 6's gradient fixed to separate the late triplet. This tests whether a cooler-temperature window can retain adequate early-pair resolution while resolving the later peaks.

Shorten the cool-temperature gradient to test whether slope changes separate the late triplet seen in injection 6. The early pair had resolution margin at 25 C, so this could reveal a faster fully resolved selectivity regime.

Return to the successful high-temperature regime and use a slope just steeper than injection 4, targeting a modest time reduction while retaining first-pair resolution. The endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution fraction of about 0.57.

Test a slightly steeper, shorter gradient near the first pair's resolution limit. The last peak will likely elute during the final hold; this run checks whether the trimmed endpoint still permits a faster fully resolved separation.

Test whether a shallower gradient restores the first-pair resolution lost at the higher starting fraction in injection 5. This maps the alternative gradient window while retaining injection 10 as the fastest fully resolved method so far.

Explore an alternative selectivity window with a higher starting fraction at 35 C. This temperature may separate the late cluster seen at 25–30 C, while the shifted solvent window tests whether adequate early-pair resolution can be recovered in a shorter run.

Test the next slightly steeper slope above injection 10 to locate the first pair's full-resolution boundary. The stronger endpoint also avoids the final-peak hold, potentially shortening the separation while preserving maximum CRF.

Reduce injection 12's slope by 25% to improve its unresolved first pair while preserving the temperature that separated the late cluster. This tests whether the cooler, higher-starting-fraction regime can achieve full resolution within 10 minutes.

Test whether a higher starting fraction changes selectivity enough to resolve the late cluster at 30 C while retaining early-pair separation. This explores a potentially faster alternative, with injection 10 retained as the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Combine the temperature that resolved the late cluster with a narrower, higher solvent window to improve resolution while trimming retention. Monitor the early pair carefully because the higher starting fraction could compress it near the dead time.

Refine the successful higher-starting-fraction method from injection 11 with a slightly steeper slope, targeting first-pair resolution just above 1.5. This should modestly shorten that separation while keeping the last peak inside the gradient.

Make the cooler method slightly shallower than injection 14 to bring its first pair above R = 1.5. The stronger endpoint should keep the last peak within 10 minutes, potentially establishing another maximum-CRF operating window.

With maximum CRF already secured, test a shallower high-temperature gradient for greater resolution margin while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes. This could provide a less marginal alternative to injection 10, whose first-pair resolution is only 1.51.

Steepen injection 19's gradient to shorten the separation while retaining more first-pair resolution margin than injection 10. The endpoint should remain above the last peak's elution fraction, avoiding a prolonged final hold.

Shorten injection 20's separation by increasing the endpoint one grid step, targeting full resolution with more margin than injection 10. This preserves the successful slope of injection 2 while trimming its unused high-organic gradient segment.

Test whether a further increase in starting organic fraction, compensated by a shallower slope, preserves full resolution at 60 C. Injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method; this run checks an alternative window rather than repeating its established slope.

Lower injection 10's endpoint one step to increase early-pair resolution while retaining the six-minute gradient. Check whether the last peak still elutes before 10 minutes during the hold, yielding a maximum-CRF alternative with more resolution margin.

Trim the successful higher-starting-fraction window to an eight-minute gradient, using a slightly shallower slope than injection 11 for additional first-pair margin. The endpoint should keep all peaks inside the gradient and preserve maximum CRF.

Lower injection 24's endpoint one step to increase first-pair resolution margin while targeting elution of all compounds before 10 minutes. Maximum CRF is already secured, and injection 10 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.
